01-physical-quantum-computation.question: An initialization prepares \(\ket\psi=a\ket0+b\ket1+c\ket\ell\) with \(|a|^2=0.60\), \(|b|^2=0.38\), and \(|c|^2=0.02\), where \(\ket\ell\) is an unwanted level. What is the probability of being in the qubit subspace, and can any later qubit gate recover the missing population?
hints: A gate on the qubit subspace acts only on \(a\) and \(b\).
01-physical-quantum-computation.answer: The qubit-subspace probability is \(0.60+0.38=0.98\). A gate defined on the qubit subspace rearranges \(a\) and \(b\) but leaves the \(\ket\ell\) component alone, so the \(2\%\) outside stays outside. Recovering it needs an operation that couples \(\ket\ell\) back, such as a leakage-reset pulse; initialization error has to be specified and corrected as a physical process, not just a qubit rotation.

01-physical-quantum-computation.question: A drive gives \(H=\hbar\Omega X/2\) with \(\Omega/(2\pi)=5\) MHz. Convert \(\Omega\) to radians per second and find the duration of a \(\pi\) rotation \(e^{-i\pi X/2}\). What duration gives a \(\pi/2\) rotation?
01-physical-quantum-computation.answer: \(\Omega=2\pi\times5\times10^6\approx3.14\times10^7\) rad/s. The evolution \(e^{-i\Omega tX/2}\) is a rotation by angle \(\Omega t\), so a \(\pi\) rotation takes \(t=\pi/\Omega=1/(2\times5\ \text{MHz})=100\) ns, and a \(\pi/2\) rotation takes \(50\) ns. Confusing \(\Omega\) with \(\Omega/2\pi\) would give durations off by a factor of \(2\pi\), a common calibration mistake.

01-physical-quantum-computation.question: A qubit with \(T_1=100\) μs idles through \(200\) sequential gates of \(50\) ns each. Compare the exact decay probability \(1-e^{-t/T_1}\) with the linear estimate \(t/T_1\). When does the linear estimate become unreliable?
01-physical-quantum-computation.answer: The total time is \(10\) μs, so \(t/T_1=0.1\). The exact decay probability is \(1-e^{-0.1}\approx0.095\), against the linear estimate \(0.100\). The difference, about \(x^2/2=0.005\), is small here but grows with \(x\); at \(t=T_1\) the linear estimate gives \(1\) while the true probability is \(0.63\). Use the exponential, or keep \(t/T_1\ll1\), when budgeting decay over long circuits.

01-physical-quantum-computation.question: A circuit has \(G=1000\) independent failure opportunities, each with probability \(p=10^{-3}\). (a) Compute the probability of at least one failure exactly and with the linear estimate \(Gp\). (b) For what \(p\) does the circuit succeed with probability \(0.9\)? (c) Name two reasons why real errors might not follow this model.
01-physical-quantum-computation.answer: (a) \(1-(0.999)^{1000}\approx0.632\), whereas \(Gp=1\), which is not even a probability. (b) \((1-p)^{1000}=0.9\) gives \(p\approx1.05\times10^{-4}\). (c) Errors can be correlated (a drifting calibration affects many gates the same way), and coherent errors add in amplitude rather than probability, so they can grow faster than this model predicts. Some errors are also harmless for a given circuit. The independent-failure model is a useful first estimate, not a law.

01-physical-quantum-computation.question: Two pulses implement \(H_A=\hbar\Omega X/2\) and \(H_B=\hbar\Omega Z/2\) alternately, each for time \(\delta t\), in place of the combined \(H_A+H_B\). (a) Using the second-order difference \(\frac{\delta t^2}{2\hbar^2}[H_A,H_B]\), estimate the size of the error for one step. (b) Evaluate it for \(\Omega\delta t=0.1\). (c) How does the error per unit of total time change if \(\delta t\) is halved?
01-physical-quantum-computation.answer: (a) \([H_A,H_B]=\frac{\hbar^2\Omega^2}{4}[X,Z]\), whose norm is \(\frac{\hbar^2\Omega^2}{2}\). The one-step error is about \(\frac{\delta t^2}{2\hbar^2}\cdot\frac{\hbar^2\Omega^2}{2}=\frac{(\Omega\delta t)^2}{4}\). (b) For \(\Omega\delta t=0.1\), about \(0.0025\) per step, which a direct matrix calculation confirms. (c) Over a fixed total time there are \(T/\delta t\) steps, so the total error scales as \(\delta t\): halving \(\delta t\) halves it, at the cost of twice as many switching events, each with its own control error.

01-physical-quantum-computation.question: A two-qubit device prepares \(\rho=\frac12\big(\ket{00}\bra{00}+\ket{11}\bra{11}+c\,\ket{00}\bra{11}+c\,\ket{11}\bra{00}\big)\) with real \(0\le c\le1\). (a) What do \(Z\)-basis population measurements show? (b) Show that \(\langle X\otimes X\rangle=c\). (c) Show that the fidelity with \((\ket{00}+\ket{11})/\sqrt2\) is \((1+c)/2\), and evaluate it for \(c=0\) and \(c=0.9\).
01-physical-quantum-computation.answer: (a) \(00\) and \(11\) each with probability \(\frac12\), for every \(c\). (b) \(\mathrm{tr}[(X\otimes X)\rho]\) picks up the off-diagonal entries, because \(X\otimes X\) swaps \(\ket{00}\) and \(\ket{11}\): \(\frac12(c+c)=c\). (c) \(F=\frac12\big(\frac12+\frac12+c\big)=\frac{1+c}{2}\): \(\frac12\) for the classical mixture and \(0.95\) for \(c=0.9\). Population measurements fix only the diagonal; a parity measurement in a rotated basis is needed to certify the coherence that makes the state a Bell pair.

01-physical-quantum-computation.question: A ten-qubit circuit has depth \(100\), with \(50\) ns per layer, and every qubit has \(T_1=100\) μs. (a) Estimate the probability that no qubit decays during the circuit. (b) Routing on a restricted connectivity doubles the depth. Recompute. (c) What does this suggest about comparing devices only by gate count?
hints: Each qubit is exposed for the whole circuit duration.
No decay on ten independent qubits: \(e^{-10t/T_1}\).
01-physical-quantum-computation.answer: (a) The duration is \(5\) μs, so each qubit survives with probability \(e^{-0.05}\) and all ten with \(e^{-0.5}\approx0.61\). (b) At depth \(200\), \(10\) μs, the probability falls to \(e^{-1}\approx0.37\). (c) Routing adds gates, but it also lengthens the circuit, and every idle qubit decays during that extra time. Depth and duration, not just the number of gates, set the exposure to decoherence, so connectivity matters even if routing gates were perfect.

01-physical-quantum-computation.question: A student writes: “The three-bit repetition encoding protects a logical qubit; with \(p=0.01\) its error is only \(3\times10^{-4}\).” Apply a single \(Z\) error on the first physical qubit to the encoded state \(\alpha\ket{000}+\beta\ket{111}\). What happens, and what does the quoted error rate actually describe?
hints: Majority decoding looks only at bit values.
01-physical-quantum-computation.answer: \(Z_1\) gives \(\alpha\ket{000}-\beta\ket{111}\): the logical relative phase has flipped. Every bit value is unchanged, so majority decoding sees nothing and the error passes through as a logical \(Z\), with probability equal to the single-qubit phase-error rate, not \(3\times10^{-4}\). The quoted figure is the logical error under independent bit flips only. A protection claim is meaningful only together with the error model it assumes.

01-physical-quantum-computation.question: A calibrated \(\pi\) pulse is too strong by \(1\%\): it rotates by \(1.01\pi\) about \(X\). (a) Find the error probability of one pulse, \(\sin^2(0.005\pi)\). (b) If the same pulse is applied \(N=100\) times where the ideal would be \(100\pi\), how large is the accumulated angle error and the resulting error probability? (c) Compare with the case where each pulse’s error has a random sign.
hints: Over-rotations about the same axis add.
Random errors add like a random walk: total angle about \(\sqrt N\) times one error.
01-physical-quantum-computation.answer: (a) A rotation error of \(0.01\pi\) leaves amplitude \(\sin(0.005\pi)\) in the wrong state: probability about \(2.5\times10^{-4}\). (b) \(100\) pulses accumulate an angle error of \(\pi\), so the qubit ends in the opposite state: error probability \(\sin^2(\pi/2)=1\). (c) With random signs, the typical accumulated angle is about \(\sqrt{100}\times0.01\pi=0.1\pi\), giving error probability about \(\sin^2(0.05\pi)\approx0.024\). Coherent (systematic) errors add in amplitude and can be far more damaging than the single-gate error rate suggests, which is why calibration must be checked with repeated sequences.

01-physical-quantum-computation.question: A Bell-pair task must succeed with probability at least \(0.99\). The circuit uses \(200\) one-qubit gates, \(100\) two-qubit gates, and \(10\) measurements. One-qubit gates fail with probability \(10^{-5}\) and measurements with \(2\times10^{-4}\). Using the small-error approximation in which failure probabilities add, find the largest two-qubit gate error rate that meets the target. What else must the specification state for this budget to be meaningful?
01-physical-quantum-computation.answer: The one-qubit gates contribute \(200\times10^{-5}=0.002\) and the measurements \(10\times2\times10^{-4}=0.002\), leaving \(0.006\) for \(100\) two-qubit gates: at most \(6\times10^{-5}\) each. The budget is meaningful only if the error rates were measured under the same conditions as the circuit (with neighbors active, the same timing, the same calibration), if errors are approximately independent and incoherent, and if idle decay, leakage, and crosstalk are included. Otherwise the sum understates the true failure probability.

02-physical-qubits.question: A qubit has \(E_1-E_0=h\times5\) GHz. Give \(\omega_{01}\) in rad/s, the time for one full cycle of relative phase, and the relative phase accumulated in \(1\) ns. Does this phase change any computational-basis probability?
02-physical-qubits.answer: \(\omega_{01}=2\pi\times5\times10^9\approx3.14\times10^{10}\) rad/s. One cycle takes \(1/f_{01}=0.2\) ns, so \(1\) ns accumulates \(10\pi\), five full cycles. The phase leaves \(|c_0|^2\) and \(|c_1|^2\) unchanged; it matters only for operations that interfere the two amplitudes, which is why drive timing and phase must be referenced to the qubit frequency.

02-physical-qubits.question: A three-level readout reports \((p_0,p_1,p_2)=(0.30,0.60,0.10)\). What does a procedure that discards level-2 events report as the probability of \(1\)? What is the unconditional probability of a valid \(1\), and what should be reported alongside it?
02-physical-qubits.answer: Discarding level \(2\) leaves \(90\%\) of the shots, among which \(1\) appears with probability \(0.60/0.90\approx0.667\). The unconditional probability of a valid \(1\) is \(0.60\). Reporting the postselected \(0.667\) without the \(10\%\) leakage fraction overstates the computational result; both numbers, or the full three-outcome distribution, should be reported.

02-physical-qubits.question: A weakly anharmonic qubit has \(\omega_{01}/2\pi=5.00\) GHz and anharmonicity \(\alpha/2\pi=-200\) MHz. Find \(\omega_{12}/2\pi\), and the detuning of a drive at \(\omega_{01}\) from the \(1\to2\) transition. Why would an equally spaced ladder be harder to control?
02-physical-qubits.answer: \(\omega_{12}/2\pi=5.00-0.20=4.80\) GHz, so a drive at \(\omega_{01}\) is detuned from the unwanted transition by \(200\) MHz. That detuning is what lets a weak, slow drive address \(0\leftrightarrow1\) while barely exciting \(1\leftrightarrow2\). With equal spacing the drive would be resonant with every transition, and frequency selection could not isolate a qubit.

02-physical-qubits.question: Use the isolated-transition bound \(\Omega^2/(\Omega^2+\Delta^2)\) for leakage to an unwanted level detuned by \(\Delta/2\pi=200\) MHz. (a) Evaluate it for \(\Omega/2\pi=20\) MHz. (b) Find the largest \(\Omega/2\pi\) that keeps the bound below \(10^{-4}\), and the corresponding \(\pi\)-pulse duration \(\pi/\Omega\). (c) With \(T_1=100\) μs, compare the decay during that pulse with the leakage target.
02-physical-qubits.answer: (a) \(\Omega/\Delta=0.1\), so the bound is \(1/101\approx0.0099\). (b) \(\Omega^2/(\Omega^2+\Delta^2)\le10^{-4}\) requires \(\Delta/\Omega\ge\sqrt{9999}\approx100\), so \(\Omega/2\pi\le2\) MHz and \(t_\pi=1/(2\times2\ \text{MHz})=250\) ns. (c) Decay during \(250\) ns is about \(2.5\times10^{-3}\), twenty-five times the leakage target. Slowing the pulse to suppress leakage increases decoherence; shaped pulses that limit spectral content at \(\Delta\) let a fast gate keep leakage small, which is why simple constant drives are rarely used.

02-physical-qubits.question: For \(H/\hbar=(\Delta Z+\Omega X)/2\) starting in \(\ket0\), use \(H^2/\hbar^2=\frac{\Omega^2+\Delta^2}{4}I\) to show that the probability of \(\ket1\) at time \(t\) is \(\frac{\Omega^2}{\Omega^2+\Delta^2}\sin^2\big(\frac{\Omega_Rt}{2}\big)\) with \(\Omega_R=\sqrt{\Omega^2+\Delta^2}\). At what times is it largest, and what are the cases \(\Delta=0\) and \(\Delta=\Omega\)?
02-physical-qubits.answer: With \(M=(\Delta Z+\Omega X)/\Omega_R\), \(M^2=I\), so \(e^{-iHt/\hbar}=\cos\frac{\Omega_Rt}{2}I-i\sin\frac{\Omega_Rt}{2}M\). Its \(\bra1\cdot\ket0\) entry is \(-i\sin\frac{\Omega_Rt}{2}\cdot\frac{\Omega}{\Omega_R}\), giving \(P_1(t)=\frac{\Omega^2}{\Omega_R^2}\sin^2\frac{\Omega_Rt}{2}\). It peaks at \(t=\pi/\Omega_R,3\pi/\Omega_R,\dots\). For \(\Delta=0\) the peak is \(1\): full Rabi oscillation. For \(\Delta=\Omega\) the peak is only \(\frac12\), and the oscillation is faster by \(\sqrt2\). Detuning both limits and speeds up the response, which is how spectroscopy locates a resonance.

02-physical-qubits.question: A qubit at \(\omega_{01}/2\pi=5.000\) GHz is driven at \(\omega_d/2\pi=5.001\) GHz. (a) In the frame rotating at \(\omega_d\), what is the residual Hamiltonian when the drive is off? (b) How much relative phase accumulates in \(250\) ns? (c) Why does this matter for a sequence of gates referenced to the drive’s phase?
02-physical-qubits.answer: (a) \(H_r=-\hbar(\omega_{01}-\omega_d)Z/2\) with \((\omega_{01}-\omega_d)/2\pi=-1\) MHz: a slow rotation about \(Z\) in the frame. (b) The phase is \(2\pi\times1\ \text{MHz}\times250\ \text{ns}=\pi/2\). (c) Gates are defined relative to the drive’s phase, so a \(\pi/2\) frame drift turns an intended \(X\) rotation into a \(Y\) rotation after \(250\) ns of idling. Even a \(1\) MHz miscalibration, \(0.02\%\) of the qubit frequency, produces a large gate error over typical circuit times.

02-physical-qubits.question: Each pulse leaves an unwanted amplitude \(\epsilon=0.01\) in a leakage level. Estimate the leaked population after \(N=10\) pulses if the amplitudes add with the same phase, and if they add with random phases. Which case does a single-pulse measurement of \(|\epsilon|^2\) predict?
hints: Random phases: populations add, giving about \(N|\epsilon|^2\).
02-physical-qubits.answer: Coherently, the amplitude grows to \(N\epsilon=0.1\), giving population \(0.01\). With random phases the populations add, giving about \(N|\epsilon|^2=10^{-3}\). A single-pulse measurement gives \(|\epsilon|^2=10^{-4}\) and says nothing about which accumulation applies. Repeating the pulse many times and watching how the leaked population grows, quadratically or linearly in \(N\), distinguishes the two cases.

02-physical-qubits.question: A student argues: “To reduce decoherence during gates, always drive harder and make pulses shorter.” Using the bound \(\Omega^2/(\Omega^2+\Delta^2)\) with \(\Delta/2\pi=200\) MHz, compare the leakage bound for \(\pi\) pulses of \(250\) ns and \(25\) ns. What is the trade-off?
02-physical-qubits.answer: A \(250\) ns pulse needs \(\Omega/2\pi=2\) MHz, with leakage bound about \(10^{-4}\). A \(25\) ns pulse needs \(20\) MHz, with bound about \(10^{-2}\), a hundred times larger, while decay during the pulse falls only tenfold. Shorter pulses reduce decoherence but excite unwanted transitions, because a fast pulse contains frequencies near \(\omega_{12}\). The optimum depends on both, and pulse shaping can move the trade-off but not remove it.

02-physical-qubits.question: For a ladder whose drive operator has matrix elements \(\bra{n+1}D\ket n\propto\sqrt{n+1}\), as for a harmonic or weakly anharmonic oscillator, the \(1\to2\) coupling is \(\sqrt2\) times the \(0\to1\) coupling. (a) Rewrite the isolated-transition leakage bound for population starting in \(\ket1\) with \(0\to1\) drive strength \(\Omega\) and anharmonicity \(\alpha\). (b) Evaluate it for \(\Omega/\alpha=0.1\). (c) Why is leakage most likely in the middle and at the end of a \(\pi\) pulse from \(\ket0\)?
hints: Leakage from \(\ket1\) requires population in \(\ket1\) first.
02-physical-qubits.answer: (a) The bound becomes \(\frac{2\Omega^2}{2\Omega^2+\alpha^2}\). (b) For \(\Omega/\alpha=0.1\): \(0.02/1.02\approx0.02\), about twice the naive estimate. (c) Leakage proceeds from \(\ket1\), which is empty at the start of a \(\pi\) pulse from \(\ket0\) and full at the end. The stronger matrix element from \(\ket1\) means that gates acting on superpositions, or repeated pulses, see larger leakage than the \(0\to1\) Rabi rate alone suggests.

02-physical-qubits.question: Two qubits on a shared control line have frequencies \(5.00\) GHz and \(5.02\) GHz. A drive at \(5.00\) GHz with \(\Omega/2\pi=10\) MHz targets the first. (a) Use the bound \(\Omega^2/(\Omega^2+\Delta^2)\) to estimate the worst-case excitation of the second qubit. (b) How far apart must the frequencies be for this crosstalk to stay below \(10^{-3}\)? (c) What does this imply for packing many qubits into a limited frequency band?
02-physical-qubits.answer: (a) \(\Delta/\Omega=2\), so the bound is \(1/(1+4)=0.2\): a large error on a qubit that should be untouched. (b) The bound falls below \(10^{-3}\) when \(\Delta/\Omega\ge31.6\), so \(\Delta/2\pi\ge316\) MHz at this drive strength (or a weaker drive). (c) Each qubit needs a clear frequency window that grows with drive strength, so a band of a few gigahertz holds only a limited number of independently addressable frequencies. This frequency crowding is one reason architectures use separate control lines, tunable frequencies, or shaped pulses.

03-coherent-control.question: A resonant pulse ramps linearly from \(0\) to a peak \(\Omega_0/2\pi=10\) MHz and back to \(0\), over a total of \(100\) ns (a triangle). Find its pulse area and the resulting excited population from \(\ket0\).
hints: The area of a triangle is half its base times its height.
03-coherent-control.answer: \(\theta=\int\Omega\,dt=\frac12\times(2\pi\times10^7\ \mathrm{s^{-1}})\times(10^{-7}\ \mathrm s)=\pi\). It is a \(\pi\) pulse, giving \(P_1=\sin^2(\pi/2)=1\). Because the axis is fixed and the Hamiltonians at different times commute, only the area matters on resonance, not the shape, which is what lets smooth envelopes replace square pulses.

03-coherent-control.question: Starting from \(\ket0\), apply a \(\pi/2\) pulse with phase \(\phi=0\), and separately one with \(\phi=\pi/2\). Using \(\cos(\theta/2)\ket0-ie^{i\phi}\sin(\theta/2)\ket1\), write both states. Do their \(Z\) populations differ?
03-coherent-control.answer: \(\phi=0\): \((\ket0-i\ket1)/\sqrt2\). \(\phi=\pi/2\): \((\ket0+\ket1)/\sqrt2=\ket+\). Both have populations \(\frac12,\frac12\), so a \(Z\) measurement cannot tell them apart; they differ by a relative phase of \(\pi/2\), which a later pulse or an \(X\)-basis measurement reveals. The drive phase selects the rotation axis.

03-coherent-control.question: A \(\pi\) pulse has a \(2\%\) amplitude error. Estimate its population failure \(\pi^2\epsilon^2/4\), and compare with the rotation-angle error itself.
03-coherent-control.answer: The population failure is about \(\pi^2(0.02)^2/4\approx9.9\times10^{-4}\). The angle error is \(\pi\epsilon\approx0.063\) rad, and the wrong-state amplitude is about \(0.031\). A single population measurement at the \(10^{-3}\) level hides an amplitude error of a few percent, which repeated sequences expose.

03-coherent-control.question: Apply an intended \(\pi\) pulse with fractional amplitude error \(\epsilon\) a total of \(N\) times (odd \(N\)), starting from \(\ket0\). (a) Show that the probability of not ending in \(\ket1\) is \(\sin^2(N\pi\epsilon/2)\). (b) Evaluate it for \(\epsilon=0.01\) with \(N=1\) and \(N=21\). (c) Why is this sequence useful for calibration?
hints: Rotations about the same axis add: total angle \(N\pi(1+\epsilon)\).
For odd \(N\), the ideal angle \(N\pi\) ends in \(\ket1\).
03-coherent-control.answer: (a) The total angle is \(N\pi+N\pi\epsilon\). For odd \(N\), \(N\pi\) alone would end in \(\ket1\), and the extra \(N\pi\epsilon\) leaves probability \(\sin^2(N\pi\epsilon/2)\) in \(\ket0\). (b) \(N=1\): \(2.5\times10^{-4}\). \(N=21\): \(\sin^2(0.33)\approx0.105\). (c) The coherent angle error grows linearly with \(N\), so the signal grows as \(N^2\epsilon^2\): a \(1\%\) error invisible in one pulse becomes a \(10\%\) effect after \(21\). Fitting the error against \(N\) calibrates the amplitude far more precisely than a single Rabi curve.

03-coherent-control.question: A drive is slightly detuned, \(\Delta=0.1\Omega\). (a) Find the maximum transfer \(\Omega^2/\Omega_R^2\). (b) Find the transfer at the resonant \(\pi\) time \(t=\pi/\Omega\). (c) How does the transfer error scale with \(\Delta/\Omega\) for small detuning, and how could a frequency error of this size be detected?
03-coherent-control.answer: (a) \(1/1.01\approx0.990\). (b) At \(t=\pi/\Omega\), \(P_1=\frac{1}{1.01}\sin^2\big(\frac\pi2\sqrt{1.01}\big)\approx0.990\): the timing mismatch costs almost nothing extra. (c) The error is about \((\Delta/\Omega)^2\), here \(1\%\), quadratic and therefore easy to miss in populations. A Ramsey sequence (two \(\pi/2\) pulses separated by a delay \(\tau\)) accumulates a phase \(\Delta\tau\) linearly in \(\Delta\), making a small frequency error visible.

03-coherent-control.question: In the weak-excitation estimate, a square pulse of duration \(T\) excites a transition detuned by \(\Delta\) in proportion to \(\mathrm{sinc}^2(\Delta T/2)\). (a) For \(\Delta/2\pi=200\) MHz, which durations put the unwanted transition at a zero of the response? (b) Evaluate the relative response at a nearby sidelobe peak, \(\Delta T/2\approx10.5\pi\). (c) Why is tuning \(T\) to a zero a fragile strategy?
03-coherent-control.answer: (a) Zeros occur at \(\Delta T/2=n\pi\), so \(T=n/(200\ \text{MHz})=5n\) ns: \(50\) ns, \(55\) ns, and so on. (b) At \(\Delta T/2=10.5\pi\), \(\mathrm{sinc}^2\approx1/(10.5\pi)^2\approx9\times10^{-4}\) of the zero-detuning weight. (c) The zero depends on the exact detuning and duration; a small drift in either moves the transition onto a sidelobe, and real pulses have rise times and nonlinear distortions. Smooth envelopes whose spectra fall off rapidly at all large detunings are more robust than relying on a zero of a square pulse.

03-coherent-control.question: Apply \(R_x(\pi/2)\) to \(\ket0\), then a \(\pi/2\) pulse about the axis \(\cos\phi X+\sin\phi Y\). (a) Show that the excited population is \(\cos^2(\phi/2)\). (b) Evaluate it at \(\phi=0,\pi/2,\pi\). (c) Explain how this sequence tests a virtual \(Z\) update.
hints: At \(\phi=0\) the two pulses make a \(\pi\) pulse; at \(\phi=\pi\) the second undoes the first.
03-coherent-control.answer: (a) The second pulse equals \(R_z(\phi)R_x(\pi/2)R_z(-\phi)\); acting on \((\ket0-i\ket1)/\sqrt2\), a direct calculation gives \(P_1=\cos^2(\phi/2)\). (b) \(\phi=0\): \(1\) (a full \(\pi\) rotation). \(\phi=\pi/2\): \(\frac12\). \(\phi=\pi\): \(0\) (the pulses cancel). (c) A virtual \(Z(\lambda)\) shifts the phase of every later pulse by \(\lambda\). Inserting it between the two pulses should move the fringe exactly as a change \(\phi\to\phi+\lambda\) predicts; a mismatch reveals an inconsistent frame. A \(Z\)-basis measurement after the first pulse alone could never see this.

03-coherent-control.question: A student says: “My \(\pi\) pulse transfers \(99.98\%\) of the population, so its error is \(2\times10^{-4}\) and it is calibrated.” Show that a \(1\%\) amplitude error gives this transfer, and identify which errors a single population measurement cannot reveal.
hints: Consider the phase of the transferred amplitude and the axis of rotation.
03-coherent-control.answer: A \(1\%\) amplitude error gives population failure \(\pi^2\epsilon^2/4\approx2.5\times10^{-4}\), consistent with the measurement. But the amplitude error is first order: the wrong-state amplitude is about \(0.016\), and in a circuit of many pulses these amplitudes add coherently. A transfer measurement also cannot see the rotation axis or a detuning-induced phase, since \(Z\) populations ignore relative phase. Calibration needs phase-sensitive and repeated sequences, not one inversion.

03-coherent-control.question: The composite pulse \(R_x(\pi/2)\,R_y(\pi)\,R_x(\pi/2)\) (applied right to left) also inverts \(\ket0\to\ket1\). Suppose every pulse has the same fractional amplitude error \(\epsilon\). A numerical calculation gives inversion failures of about \(6\times10^{-8}\), \(4\times10^{-5}\), and \(6\times10^{-4}\) for \(\epsilon=0.01,0.05,0.1\), compared with \(2.5\times10^{-4}\), \(6.2\times10^{-3}\), and \(2.4\times10^{-2}\) for a single \(\pi\) pulse. (a) How do the two failures scale with \(\epsilon\)? (b) What is the cost? (c) Why is a pulse robust for inversion not necessarily robust as a gate on arbitrary states?
hints: Compare the ratios when \(\epsilon\) is multiplied by \(5\).
Robust population transfer does not guarantee a correct phase.
03-coherent-control.answer: (a) Multiplying \(\epsilon\) by \(5\) multiplies the single-pulse failure by about \(25\) (quadratic) and the composite failure by about \(600\approx5^4\) (quartic). At \(\epsilon=0.01\) the composite pulse is about \(4000\) times better. (b) It takes twice the total rotation, hence twice the time and twice the exposure to decoherence and detuning. (c) The composite pulse is designed to map \(\ket0\) to \(\ket1\) robustly; on other inputs its residual error can include phases that do not cancel. A gate must be robust as a unitary, which requires a different and usually longer composite sequence.

03-coherent-control.question: In the weak-excitation estimate, compare the leakage weight of a square pulse with that of a Gaussian pulse \(\Omega(t)\propto e^{-t^2/2\sigma^2}\), whose spectral weight at detuning \(\Delta\) falls as \(e^{-\Delta^2\sigma^2}\). Take \(\Delta/2\pi=200\) MHz, a square pulse of \(T=52\) ns (a sidelobe), and a Gaussian with \(\sigma=10\) ns. Estimate the two relative weights and explain the difference.
03-coherent-control.answer: For the square pulse, \(\mathrm{sinc}^2(10.5\pi)\approx9\times10^{-4}\): its spectrum falls only as \(1/(\Delta T)^2\) because of its sharp edges. For the Gaussian, \(e^{-(12.6)^2}\approx10^{-69}\), utterly negligible in this estimate. Smooth envelopes concentrate their spectrum near the carrier. In practice the limit is set instead by finite pulse duration, truncation of the Gaussian tails, and distortions in the control electronics, which is why measured leakage is never as small as the ideal Gaussian estimate.

04-qubit-interactions.question: Under \(H=\hbar JZ\otimes Z/2\), the four basis phases after time \(t\) are \(e^{\mp iJt/2}\). Evaluate the local-correction-proof combination \(\phi_{00}-\phi_{01}-\phi_{10}+\phi_{11}\), and find the time that gives a controlled-\(Z\) (up to local phases) for \(J/2\pi=1\) MHz.
hints: Energies are \(+\hbar J/2\) on \(00,11\) and \(-\hbar J/2\) on \(01,10\).
04-qubit-interactions.answer: The phases are \(\phi_{00}=\phi_{11}=-Jt/2\) and \(\phi_{01}=\phi_{10}=+Jt/2\), so the combination is \(-2Jt\). A controlled-\(Z\) needs this combination to equal \(\pi\) modulo \(2\pi\), that is \(Jt=\pi/2\): \(t=\pi/(2J)=1/(4\times1\ \text{MHz})=250\) ns. The rest of the phases are removed by single-qubit \(Z\) rotations.

04-qubit-interactions.question: For the exchange interaction \(H=\hbar g(XX+YY)/2\) with \(g/2\pi=2\) MHz, how long does a full swap \(\ket{01}\to\ket{10}\) take, and how long does the entangling half-swap take? What state does the half-swap make from \(\ket{01}\)?
04-qubit-interactions.answer: Full transfer needs \(gt=\pi/2\): \(t=1/(4\times2\ \text{MHz})=125\) ns. The half-swap at \(gt=\pi/4\) takes \(62.5\) ns and gives \((\ket{01}-i\ket{10})/\sqrt2\), a maximally entangled state with a definite relative phase \(-i\). The states \(\ket{00}\) and \(\ket{11}\) are untouched by this interaction.

04-qubit-interactions.question: A mediator ends a gate in coherent states that differ by \(\Delta\alpha\) between two data branches. Find the remaining fraction of coherence, \(e^{-|\Delta\alpha|^2/2}\), for \(\Delta\alpha=0.5\) and \(\Delta\alpha=1\). How small must \(|\Delta\alpha|\) be to keep \(99.9\%\)?
04-qubit-interactions.answer: \(e^{-0.125}\approx0.88\) and \(e^{-0.5}\approx0.61\). Keeping \(99.9\%\) requires \(|\Delta\alpha|^2\le-2\ln0.999\approx0.002\), so \(|\Delta\alpha|\lesssim0.045\). The mediator must return to its starting state to within a few hundredths of a displacement unit; a gate that leaves the oscillator slightly displaced degrades the data coherence even when all data populations are correct.

04-qubit-interactions.question: Build a CNOT (control qubit 1, target qubit 2) from the ZZ interaction. (a) Show that \(H_2\,\mathrm{CZ}\,H_2\) is CNOT by checking its action on \(\ket{10}\) and \(\ket{11}\). (b) List the full sequence, starting from \(e^{-iJtZZ/2}\) with \(Jt=\pi/2\). (c) Apply it to \(\ket{+}\ket0\).
hints: From Section 4.2.1, CZ is the ZZ evolution followed by \(R_z(-\pi/2)\) on each qubit.
04-qubit-interactions.answer: (a) On the control-\(1\) branch, CZ applies \(Z\) to the target, and \(HZH=X\); on the control-\(0\) branch it applies \(I\), and \(HIH=I\). So \(H_2\,\mathrm{CZ}\,H_2\) flips the target exactly when the control is \(1\): \(\ket{10}\to\ket{11}\), \(\ket{11}\to\ket{10}\). (b) \(H\) on qubit 2; ZZ evolution for \(Jt=\pi/2\); \(R_z(-\pi/2)\) on both qubits; \(H\) on qubit 2. (c) From \(\ket+\ket0\) the result is \((\ket{00}+\ket{11})/\sqrt2\), the Bell state of Chapter 1, up to a global phase.

04-qubit-interactions.question: Two devices implement the same truth table on \(00,01,10,11\): device A performs CNOT, and device B performs CNOT followed by CZ. (a) Show that they agree on every basis input. (b) Apply both to \(\ket+\ket0\) and compare the outputs. (c) What test distinguishes them?
hints: CZ changes only the sign of \(\ket{11}\).
04-qubit-interactions.answer: (a) CZ only multiplies \(\ket{11}\) by \(-1\), which changes no basis-state population, so both devices map each basis input to the same basis output. (b) A gives \((\ket{00}+\ket{11})/\sqrt2\); B gives \((\ket{00}-\ket{11})/\sqrt2\). These are orthogonal: on this input the devices produce perfectly distinguishable outputs. (c) Prepare superpositions and measure phase-sensitive observables, for example \(\langle X\otimes X\rangle\), which is \(+1\) for A’s output and \(-1\) for B’s. Process tomography or interleaved benchmarking does this systematically; a truth table cannot.

04-qubit-interactions.question: Use the toy error model \(\epsilon(t)=at+b/t^2\) with \(a=1/T_1=10^4\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}\) and \(b=10^{-19}\ \mathrm{s^2}\). (a) Find the optimal gate time and the minimum error. (b) Compare with \(t=50\) ns. (c) Explain the two terms physically and why the optimum is shallow.
04-qubit-interactions.answer: (a) \(t^*=(2\times10^{-19}/10^4)^{1/3}\approx27\) ns, giving \(\epsilon\approx2.7\times10^{-4}+1.4\times10^{-4}\approx4.1\times10^{-4}\). (b) At \(50\) ns, \(\epsilon=5\times10^{-4}+4\times10^{-5}=5.4\times10^{-4}\). (c) The first term models decay during the gate, growing with duration; the second models off-resonant errors that grow with the drive strength needed for a fixed area. Near the optimum the error changes slowly, so a range of durations performs similarly, and other constraints, such as crosstalk and bandwidth, often decide the choice.

04-qubit-interactions.question: For \(H=\hbar JZ\otimes Z/2\) acting for time \(t\) on \(\ket{++}\), (a) write the four amplitudes; (b) use the determinant of the two-by-two amplitude table from Section 4.2.1, \(|\alpha_{00}\alpha_{11}-\alpha_{01}\alpha_{10}|\), to find how entangled the output is as a function of \(Jt\); (c) at which \(Jt\) is the entanglement largest, and when does it vanish?
04-qubit-interactions.answer: (a) \(\frac12\big(e^{-iJt/2},e^{iJt/2},e^{iJt/2},e^{-iJt/2}\big)\). (b) \(\alpha_{00}\alpha_{11}-\alpha_{01}\alpha_{10}=\frac14(e^{-iJt}-e^{iJt})=-\frac i2\sin Jt\), with magnitude \(\frac12|\sin Jt|\). (c) It is largest, \(\frac12\) (maximal entanglement, as for a Bell state), at \(Jt=\pi/2\), the CZ point, and zero at \(Jt=0,\pi,\dots\), where the evolution is a product of local phase gates. An interaction left on twice as long as intended undoes its own entangling action.

04-qubit-interactions.question: A student checks a mediated gate by verifying that the oscillator’s mean phonon number returns to its initial value in both data branches, and concludes that the mediator is disentangled. Explain why this can fail for coherent states \(\ket{\alpha}\) and \(\ket{-\alpha}\), and compute the remaining data coherence for \(\alpha=0.3\).
hints: \(\ket\alpha\) and \(\ket{-\alpha}\) have the same mean phonon number \(|\alpha|^2\).
04-qubit-interactions.answer: \(\ket{\alpha}\) and \(\ket{-\alpha}\) have the same mean phonon number \(|\alpha|^2\), so a population check sees nothing wrong, yet the two states are different and partly distinguishable. The data coherence is multiplied by \(|\braket{-\alpha}{\alpha}|=e^{-|2\alpha|^2/2}=e^{-0.18}\approx0.84\) for \(\alpha=0.3\). Disentanglement requires the mediator states in the two branches to be the same state, not merely to have the same energy; it is tested by interference on the data or by measuring the mediator’s phase-sensitive observables.

04-qubit-interactions.question: Two qubits coupled by exchange have frequencies differing by \(\delta\). In the one-excitation subspace \(\{\ket{01},\ket{10}\}\), the Hamiltonian is \(\hbar\begin{pmatrix}\delta/2&g\\g&-\delta/2\end{pmatrix}\). (a) Using the detuned Rabi formula, find the maximum swap probability. (b) Evaluate it for \(\delta=0\), \(\delta=2g\), and \(\delta=20g\). (c) How can this be used to switch an always-on coupling on and off?
hints: This matrix has the same form as \((\Delta Z+\Omega X)/2\) with \(\Omega=2g\), \(\Delta=\delta\).
04-qubit-interactions.answer: (a) Matching to \((\Delta Z+\Omega X)/2\) gives \(\Omega=2g\), \(\Delta=\delta\), so the maximum swap probability is \(\frac{4g^2}{4g^2+\delta^2}\). (b) \(\delta=0\): \(1\). \(\delta=2g\): \(\frac12\). \(\delta=20g\): \(\frac{4}{404}\approx0.01\). (c) Tuning the qubits into resonance turns the exchange on; detuning them far apart suppresses it, leaving only a small residual (and a second-order ZZ shift). Tunable-frequency qubits use this to implement two-qubit gates on demand with a fixed coupler.

04-qubit-interactions.question: A mediated gate is designed so that the oscillator trajectory closes at \(T=2\pi/|\delta|\), but the pulse ends a little late, at \(T+\tau\). Near closure, the displacement difference between branches grows roughly as \(\Delta\alpha\approx2g\tau\) for a force of strength \(g\) on observable values \(s=\pm1\). (a) For \(g/2\pi=50\) kHz, what timing error \(\tau\) keeps the coherence above \(0.999\)? (b) What does this imply about timing precision relative to the gate duration if \(\delta/2\pi=200\) kHz?
04-qubit-interactions.answer: (a) \(|\Delta\alpha|=2g\tau\le0.045\) gives \(\tau\le0.045/(2\times2\pi\times5\times10^4\ \mathrm{s^{-1}})\approx72\) ns. (b) With \(T=5\) μs, the timing must be correct to about \(1.4\%\) of the gate duration. The tolerance tightens as the force strengthens, so faster mediated gates demand proportionally more precise timing, and frequency drifts in \(\delta\) shift the closure time in the same way. (These estimates use the stated scaling; an exact treatment uses the full phase-space trajectory.)

05-initialization-and-readout.question: For a \(5\) GHz qubit, \(hf/k_B\approx0.240\) K. Using \(p_1=1/(1+e^{hf/k_BT})\), find the thermal excited population at an effective temperature of \(50\) mK and of \(100\) mK. What does the comparison say about a hot qubit in a cold refrigerator?
05-initialization-and-readout.answer: At \(50\) mK, \(p_1=1/(1+e^{4.8})\approx0.008\); at \(100\) mK, \(p_1=1/(1+e^{2.4})\approx0.083\). Doubling the effective temperature raises the excited population tenfold. The qubit’s effective temperature is set by its coupling to everything, including stray radiation, not just the refrigerator reading, so it must be inferred from measured populations.

05-initialization-and-readout.question: A detector has \(e_0=0.05\) and \(e_1=0.10\). If the true excited population is \(p=0.3\), what fraction of shots reports \(1\)? If \(60\%\) of shots report \(1\), what population does the assignment model infer?
05-initialization-and-readout.answer: Reported fraction: \(0.05+0.85\times0.3=0.305\). Inverting, \(p=(0.60-0.05)/0.85\approx0.647\). The inversion is valid only if \(e_0,e_1\) were calibrated under the same conditions, and the factor \(1/0.85\) also amplifies statistical noise in the reported fraction.

05-initialization-and-readout.question: A readout records independent samples with mean separation \(0.2\sigma_0\) per sample. With a midpoint threshold and equal priors, each assignment error is \(Q(d/2)\), where \(d\) is the separation in units of the averaged noise and \(Q(3.09)\approx10^{-3}\). How many samples \(M\) are needed for an assignment error of \(10^{-3}\)?
05-initialization-and-readout.answer: Averaging \(M\) samples gives \(d=0.2\sqrt M\). Requiring \(d/2=3.09\) gives \(d=6.18\) and \(M=(6.18/0.2)^2\approx955\) samples. The error falls rapidly with \(M\) once \(d\) is a few units, but only if the state does not change during the record, which the next exercises examine.

05-initialization-and-readout.question: Active reset measures the qubit and applies \(X\) on outcome \(1\). The initial excited population is \(p=0.1\), and the assignment errors are \(e_0=0.01\), \(e_1=0.05\). (a) Find the residual excited population after an ideal conditional \(X\). (b) If the feedback takes \(\tau=1\) μs and \(T_1=50\) μs, how does relaxation during the delay change the result? (c) Compare with waiting \(5T_1\) for thermal relaxation to \(p_{\rm eq}=0.005\).
hints: Errors: a ground state wrongly flipped, or an excited state wrongly left alone.
During the delay, an excited state reported as \(1\) may decay before the \(X\) flips it back up.
05-initialization-and-readout.answer: (a) Residual \(=(1-p)e_0+pe_1=0.009+0.005=0.014\). (b) An excited qubit correctly reported as \(1\) decays during the delay with probability about \(\tau/T_1=0.02\); the \(X\) then flips it from \(\ket0\) to \(\ket1\). This adds about \(p(1-e_1)\times0.02\approx0.002\), for a total near \(0.016\). (c) Waiting \(5T_1=250\) μs gives about \(p_{\rm eq}+pe^{-5}\approx0.0057\), better but \(250\) times slower. Reset quality depends on assignment, latency, and the thermal floor together.

05-initialization-and-readout.question: An experiment reports \(1\) on a fraction \(\hat r\) of \(N=10^4\) shots and infers \(p=(\hat r-e_0)/(1-e_0-e_1)\). (a) If \(\hat r\approx0.5\), find the statistical standard deviation of \(\hat r\). (b) Propagate it to the inferred \(p\) for \(e_0+e_1=0.1\) and for \(e_0+e_1=0.8\). (c) What happens as \(e_0+e_1\to1\)?
hints: The standard deviation of a binomial fraction is \(\sqrt{\hat r(1-\hat r)/N}\).
05-initialization-and-readout.answer: (a) \(\sqrt{0.25/10^4}=0.005\). (b) With \(1-e_0-e_1=0.9\), the inferred \(p\) has standard deviation about \(0.0056\); with \(0.2\), about \(0.025\), five times worse than the raw fraction. (c) As \(e_0+e_1\to1\) the detector output stops depending on the qubit, the inversion divides by nearly zero, and both statistical and calibration errors blow up. Assignment correction is reliable only for a reasonably good detector.

05-initialization-and-readout.question: Two equal-width Gaussian signal distributions have means \(\mu_0=0\) and \(\mu_1=4\sigma\). The prior probability of \(\ket0\) is \(0.9\). (a) Find the optimal threshold, where \(0.9f_0(s)=0.1f_1(s)\). (b) Compare with the midpoint \(2\sigma\). (c) Why does the threshold move toward \(\mu_1\)?
05-initialization-and-readout.answer: (a) Solving gives \(s^*=\frac{\mu_0+\mu_1}{2}+\frac{\sigma^2\ln(0.9/0.1)}{\mu_1-\mu_0}=2\sigma+\frac{\ln9}{4}\sigma\approx2.55\sigma\). (b) The threshold moves \(0.55\sigma\) above the midpoint. (c) Since \(\ket0\) is nine times more likely, a signal near the midpoint is more probably a noisy \(\ket0\) than a \(\ket1\), so the rule demands stronger evidence before reporting \(1\). This is the same Bayesian reasoning as Bob’s lamp in a discrete setting: the optimal decision depends on priors as well as the response distributions.

05-initialization-and-readout.question: A qubit prepared in \(\ket1\) is measured twice, with separation \(\tau\). Each report has symmetric assignment error \(e=0.01\), and the qubit decays with \(T_1=100\) μs between reports. (a) Estimate the probability that the two reports disagree for \(\tau=0\) and \(\tau=1\) μs. (b) How would measuring the disagreement as a function of \(\tau\) separate the two mechanisms?
05-initialization-and-readout.answer: (a) At \(\tau=0\), disagreement comes only from assignment: about \(2e(1-e)\approx0.020\). At \(\tau=1\) μs, decay between the reports adds about \(\tau/T_1=0.01\), for roughly \(0.030\). (b) Assignment errors give a constant offset independent of \(\tau\), while relaxation adds a part growing as \(1-e^{-\tau/T_1}\). Fitting the disagreement against \(\tau\) separates them; transitions induced by the measurement itself appear as a \(\tau\)-independent excess beyond the calibrated assignment error.

05-initialization-and-readout.question: A student says: “Integrating the readout signal longer always improves assignment, because the noise falls as \(1/\sqrt M\).” With \(T_1=50\) μs and an integration window of \(2\) μs, estimate the error floor from decay during the window. What limits the useful integration time?
hints: A decay partway through the window is misassigned roughly half the time.
The decay probability during the window is about \(\tau/T_1\).
05-initialization-and-readout.answer: The probability of decaying during a \(2\) μs window is about \(\tau/T_1=0.04\), and a qubit that decays partway through gives a signal between the calibrated distributions, misassigned roughly half the time: an error floor near \(2\%\) for excited inputs. Longer integration reduces the Gaussian overlap but increases this floor. The useful window balances noise averaging against relaxation (and against drifts and correlations in the amplifier noise), and is usually much shorter than \(T_1\).

05-initialization-and-readout.question: Model the assignment error of an excited input as \(Q\big(k\sqrt\tau/2\big)+\tau/(2T_1)\), with \(k=6.32\ \mu\mathrm s^{-1/2}\) and \(T_1=50\) μs. (a) Evaluate it at \(\tau=0.1\) μs and \(\tau=2\) μs. (b) A numerical minimization gives an optimum near \(\tau\approx0.85\) μs with error about \(0.010\). Check the two contributions there. (c) How would a qubit with \(T_1=500\) μs change the optimum?
hints: A longer \(T_1\) lowers the decay term.
05-initialization-and-readout.answer: (a) At \(0.1\) μs: \(Q(1.0)+0.001\approx0.16\), dominated by overlap. At \(2\) μs: \(Q(4.47)+0.02\approx0.020\), dominated by decay. (b) At \(0.85\) μs, \(k\sqrt\tau/2\approx2.91\), giving \(Q\approx0.0018\), plus \(0.85/100=0.0085\), totalling about \(0.010\). (c) With \(T_1=500\) μs the decay term is ten times smaller, so the optimum shifts to a longer window (about \(1.5\) to \(2\) μs in this model) and the minimum error falls to a few parts in \(10^3\). Readout fidelity is limited jointly by signal-to-noise ratio and qubit lifetime.

05-initialization-and-readout.question: Heralded initialization measures the qubit and keeps only runs that report \(0\). With thermal excited population \(p=0.08\), \(e_0=0.02\), and \(e_1=0.05\), (a) find the fraction of runs kept; (b) use Bayes’ rule to find the probability that a kept run is actually excited; (c) compare with the unheralded \(p\), and state the costs of this method.
05-initialization-and-readout.answer: (a) \(P(0)=0.92\times0.98+0.08\times0.05=0.9016+0.004=0.9056\): about \(91\%\) of runs are kept. (b) \(P(\text{excited}\mid0)=0.004/0.9056\approx0.0044\). (c) Heralding reduces the excited population from \(8\%\) to about \(0.44\%\), limited by \(e_1\). It costs \(9\%\) of the runs, a measurement’s duration, and possible measurement-induced disturbance, so the measurement must be nondemolition: it must leave a qubit reported as \(0\) actually in \(\ket0\).

06-noise-and-decoherence.question: A qubit has \(T_1=50\) μs and an independent pure-dephasing time \(T_\phi=200\) μs. Find \(T_2\) in the exponential model, and the coherence remaining after \(20\) μs.
06-noise-and-decoherence.answer: \(1/T_2=1/100+1/200=3/200\ \mu\mathrm s^{-1}\), so \(T_2\approx66.7\) μs. After \(20\) μs the coherence factor is \(e^{-0.3}\approx0.74\). Relaxation alone would give \(T_2=100\) μs; the dephasing makes it shorter, and no process in this model can push it above \(2T_1\).

06-noise-and-decoherence.question: A qubit with \(\hbar\omega/k_BT=4.8\) relaxes downward at rate \(\Gamma_\downarrow=1/(50\ \mu\mathrm s)\) and obeys detailed balance. Find \(\Gamma_\uparrow\), the equilibrium population, and the observed relaxation rate toward equilibrium.
06-noise-and-decoherence.answer: \(\Gamma_\uparrow=\Gamma_\downarrow e^{-4.8}\approx0.0082\,\Gamma_\downarrow\). The equilibrium population is \(\Gamma_\uparrow/(\Gamma_\uparrow+\Gamma_\downarrow)\approx0.0081\), and the approach to equilibrium has rate \(\Gamma_\uparrow+\Gamma_\downarrow\approx1.008\Gamma_\downarrow\), only \(0.8\%\) faster than \(\Gamma_\downarrow\) alone. The upward rate barely changes the measured lifetime but sets a floor on the ground-state preparation.

06-noise-and-decoherence.question: Shot-to-shot frequency noise gives a zero-mean Gaussian accumulated phase with variance \(v\). Find the Ramsey contrast for \(v=0.5\ \mathrm{rad}^2\) and \(v=2\ \mathrm{rad}^2\). Is any individual run decohered?
hints: Each run has a definite (but unknown) phase.
06-noise-and-decoherence.answer: \(e^{-0.25}\approx0.78\) and \(e^{-1}\approx0.37\). No individual run need be mixed: each acquires a definite but random phase, and the reduced contrast comes from averaging runs with different phases. That is why such dephasing can be partly undone by an echo, unlike energy loss to the environment.

06-noise-and-decoherence.question: In a Ramsey experiment with detuning \(\Delta/2\pi=100\) kHz and \(T_2=50\) μs, the probability of \(+\) is \(\frac12\big[1+e^{-t/T_2}\cos(\Delta t)\big]\). (a) Evaluate it at \(t=2.5\) μs and \(t=5\) μs. (b) A student fits the data at these two points with a decay alone, ignoring the cosine. What would they wrongly conclude? (c) How should the experiment be designed to separate frequency error from decoherence?
hints: \(\Delta t=\pi/2\) at \(2.5\) μs and \(\pi\) at \(5\) μs.
06-noise-and-decoherence.answer: (a) At \(2.5\) μs, \(\cos(\pi/2)=0\), so \(P(+)=0.5\). At \(5\) μs, \(\cos\pi=-1\), so \(P(+)=\frac12(1-0.905)\approx0.048\). (b) A pure-decay fit would read \(P(+)=0.5\) as complete loss of coherence after \(2.5\) μs, a \(T_2\) twenty times too short, and could not explain \(P(+)<0.5\) at all. (c) Sample many delays to resolve the oscillation and fit frequency and envelope together, or deliberately detune by a known amount so that the fringe frequency and its decay are both measured.

06-noise-and-decoherence.question: A qubit’s frequency offset is constant during each run but varies from run to run with standard deviation \(\sigma_\omega/2\pi=10\) kHz (Gaussian). (a) Show that the Ramsey contrast is \(e^{-\sigma_\omega^2t^2/2}\), and find the time \(T_2^*\) at which it falls to \(e^{-1}\). (b) What does a Hahn echo do to this noise, and what limits the echo contrast?
hints: An echo refocuses an offset that is constant during the run.
06-noise-and-decoherence.answer: (a) The phase is \(\delta\omega\,t\), Gaussian with variance \(v=\sigma_\omega^2t^2\), so the contrast is \(e^{-\sigma_\omega^2t^2/2}\), a Gaussian envelope. It reaches \(e^{-1}\) at \(T_2^*=\sqrt2/\sigma_\omega\approx\sqrt2/(2\pi\times10^4\ \mathrm{s^{-1}})\approx22.5\) μs. (b) An echo cancels a run-constant offset exactly, so this noise contributes nothing to the echo signal. The echo contrast is limited by relaxation (\(e^{-t/2T_1}\)), by noise that changes within a run, and by imperfect \(\pi\) pulses. Comparing Ramsey and echo separates slow from fast noise.

06-noise-and-decoherence.question: Two neighboring qubits each flip with probability \(p=0.01\) per cycle. (a) Compare the probability that both flip if the flips are independent and if they come from one shared event. (b) A three-qubit repetition code is built on qubits that flip together through a shared event with probability \(p\). What is the logical error per cycle, compared with \(3p^2\) for independent flips? (c) What measurement reveals the difference?
hints: Shared event: all three flip together with probability \(p\).
Marginal flip probabilities are identical in both models.
06-noise-and-decoherence.answer: (a) Independent: \(p^2=10^{-4}\). Shared: \(p=10^{-2}\), a hundred times larger. (b) If a shared event flips all three code qubits, majority decoding fails every time it happens: logical error \(p=10^{-2}\), compared with about \(3\times10^{-4}\) for independent flips. The code is useless against fully correlated noise. (c) Single-qubit error rates are the same in both models; only simultaneous measurements of several qubits, comparing joint flip rates with products of marginals, expose the correlation.

06-noise-and-decoherence.question: A qubit prepared in \(\ket1\) relaxes toward \(p_{\rm eq}=0.05\): \(p_1(t)=p_{\rm eq}+(1-p_{\rm eq})e^{-t/T_1}\). (a) Evaluate \(p_1\) at \(t=T_1\). (b) A fit that assumes \(p_{\rm eq}=0\) infers a lifetime from this point as \(-t/\ln p_1\). What lifetime does it report? (c) How do measurements starting from both \(\ket0\) and \(\ket1\) remove the bias?
06-noise-and-decoherence.answer: (a) \(p_1(T_1)=0.05+0.95\times0.368\approx0.399\). (b) \(-T_1/\ln0.399\approx1.09T_1\): the lifetime is overestimated by about \(9\%\), and the bias grows at later times, where the floor dominates. (c) Starting from \(\ket0\), the population rises toward the same \(p_{\rm eq}\) with the same rate. Fitting both curves together fixes the floor and the common rate, so neither is confused with the other.

06-noise-and-decoherence.question: A student models leakage as an extra depolarizing error with the same probability. Suppose a gate leaks with probability \(10^{-3}\), and a leaked qubit stays leaked for the next \(20\) gates, during which every gate involving it fails. Compare the number of failed gates caused by one leakage event with one Pauli error, and explain what the depolarizing model misses.
hints: A Pauli error affects one gate; persistent leakage affects every later gate until removal.
Two-qubit gates also spread errors to partners.
06-noise-and-decoherence.answer: A Pauli error is a single event: it corrupts one gate’s output, and later gates act normally. A leaked qubit corrupts all \(20\) subsequent gates that use it, and in two-qubit gates it can disturb its partners too. So one leakage event can cause twenty or more failures, while the depolarizing model counts one. The model misses memory: leakage persists until a dedicated removal step. Error rates must specify whether failures are independent per gate or can persist and spread.

06-noise-and-decoherence.question: Echo phase is \(\int y(t)\,\delta\omega(t)\,dt\), where \(y=\pm1\) switches sign at each \(\pi\) pulse. Consider a frequency offset drifting linearly during a run, \(\delta\omega(t)=\beta t\), over total time \(t_f\). (a) Show that a single echo (pulse at \(t_f/2\)) leaves phase \(-\beta t_f^2/4\). (b) Show that two pulses at \(t_f/4\) and \(3t_f/4\) cancel the linear drift. (c) What general principle about pulse sequences does this illustrate?
hints: For one pulse, integrate \(\beta t\) from \(0\) to \(t_f/2\), then subtract from \(t_f/2\) to \(t_f\).
For two pulses, \(y=+1,-1,+1\) on the three intervals.
06-noise-and-decoherence.answer: (a) \(\beta\big[\frac{t_f^2}{8}-\big(\frac{t_f^2}{2}-\frac{t_f^2}{8}\big)\big]=-\frac{\beta t_f^2}{4}\neq0\). (b) With \(y=+1\) on \([0,t_f/4]\), \(-1\) on \([t_f/4,3t_f/4]\), \(+1\) on \([3t_f/4,t_f]\): \(\frac\beta2\big[\frac{1}{16}-\frac{8}{16}+\frac{7}{16}\big]t_f^2=0\). (c) A sequence cancels noise components whose time dependence is orthogonal to its switching function \(y(t)\): one pulse removes constant offsets, two symmetric pulses also remove linear drifts. More pulses suppress progressively faster noise, at the cost of more pulse errors. This is the idea behind dynamical decoupling and noise spectroscopy.

06-noise-and-decoherence.question: A Ramsey contrast is measured at times \(t_1\) and \(2t_1\). Show that for an exponential envelope \(C(2t_1)=C(t_1)^2\), while for a Gaussian envelope \(C(2t_1)=C(t_1)^4\). If \(C(t_1)=0.8\) and \(C(2t_1)=0.42\), which model fits better, and what does that suggest about the noise?
06-noise-and-decoherence.answer: For \(C=e^{-t/T}\), doubling \(t\) squares \(C\). For \(C=e^{-(t/T)^2}\), doubling \(t\) multiplies the exponent by four, raising \(C\) to the fourth power. The data give \(0.42\), close to \(0.8^4\approx0.41\) and far from \(0.8^2=0.64\): the decay is Gaussian. That points to slow, quasi-static frequency noise, which a Hahn echo should largely refocus, rather than fast Markovian dephasing, which an echo would not remove.

07-calibration-and-characterization.question: A Ramsey fringe has a period of \(4\) μs. What is \(|\Delta|/2\pi\)? Why does a cosine-only trace not determine whether the qubit is above or below the drive frequency?
07-calibration-and-characterization.answer: \(|\Delta|/2\pi=1/(4\ \mu\mathrm s)=0.25\) MHz. The trace depends on \(\cos(\Delta t+\phi_0)\), and with \(\phi_0=0\) the values for \(+\Delta\) and \(-\Delta\) coincide. Measuring with a second analysis phase, which gives the sine, or repeating with a deliberately shifted drive frequency, reveals the sign.

07-calibration-and-characterization.question: Tomography gives \(\langle X\rangle=0.6\), \(\langle Y\rangle=0\), \(\langle Z\rangle=0.6\). Write \(\rho\), check that it is physical, and find its purity \(\mathrm{tr}\rho^2=\frac12(1+|\vec r|^2)\).
07-calibration-and-characterization.answer: \(\rho=\frac12\begin{pmatrix}1.6&0.6\\0.6&0.4\end{pmatrix}\). The Bloch length is \(\sqrt{0.72}\approx0.85\le1\), so it is physical. The purity is \(\frac12(1+0.72)=0.86\): a partly mixed state lying between \(\ket0\) and \(\ket+\) on the Bloch sphere.

07-calibration-and-characterization.question: Randomized benchmarking fits \(\alpha=0.995\) per Clifford. Find the depolarizing-model error per Clifford. If an average Clifford is compiled into \(1.875\) native pulses, what rough error per native pulse does this suggest, and what assumption does that division make?
hints: Division assumes errors add equally per pulse.
07-calibration-and-characterization.answer: Error per Clifford is \((1-0.995)/2=2.5\times10^{-3}\). Dividing by \(1.875\) suggests about \(1.3\times10^{-3}\) per native pulse. That assumes every native pulse contributes equally and independently, which fails if some pulses (or the idle periods between them) are much worse than others. Per-pulse error needs a separate experiment, such as interleaved benchmarking.

07-calibration-and-characterization.question: Finite-shot tomography gives \(\langle X\rangle=0.70\), \(\langle Y\rangle=0.10\), \(\langle Z\rangle=0.75\). (a) Compute the Bloch length and the smallest eigenvalue \((1-|\vec r|)/2\) of the estimated \(\rho\). (b) With \(1000\) shots per basis, is the excess consistent with sampling noise? (c) What should be reported instead of the raw estimate?
hints: The standard deviation of an expectation from \(N\) shots is about \(\sqrt{(1-\langle\cdot\rangle^2)/N}\).
07-calibration-and-characterization.answer: (a) \(|\vec r|\approx1.031\), so the smallest eigenvalue is about \(-0.015\): the raw estimate is not a valid density matrix. (b) The standard deviations are about \(\sqrt{0.51/1000}\approx0.023\) for \(X\) and \(\sqrt{0.44/1000}\approx0.021\) for \(Z\), so an overshoot of \(0.03\) in length is about one standard deviation: consistent with sampling noise around a nearly pure state. (c) A constrained (for example maximum-likelihood) estimate restricted to \(|\vec r|\le1\), together with uncertainty estimates, rather than an unphysical matrix.

07-calibration-and-characterization.question: A benchmarking experiment fits \(A\alpha^m+B\) with \(B=0.5\). Measured survivals are \(0.772\) at \(m=50\) and \(0.665\) at \(m=100\). (a) Extract \(\alpha\) without knowing \(A\). (b) Find \(A\) and the error per Clifford. (c) Why is it useful that \(\alpha\) is extracted from the decay rather than from a single sequence length?
07-calibration-and-characterization.answer: (a) \(\alpha^{50}=(0.665-0.5)/(0.772-0.5)\approx0.607\), so \(\alpha\approx0.607^{1/50}\approx0.990\). (b) \(A=0.272/0.990^{50}\approx0.45\), and the error per Clifford is \((1-0.990)/2\approx5\times10^{-3}\). (c) Preparation and measurement errors affect \(A\) and \(B\) but not the rate of decay with \(m\); comparing sequence lengths separates per-gate error from fixed state-preparation and readout errors, which a single-length survival would mix together.

07-calibration-and-characterization.question: After \(m\) repeated identity gates, the measured excited population is \(0.100\) at \(m=0\), \(0.120\) at \(m=10\), and \(0.140\) at \(m=20\). (a) Fit a straight line and interpret the slope and intercept. (b) Can the intercept be split into preparation and readout errors from these data alone? (c) Propose an additional measurement that would help.
hints: Both preparation and readout errors appear at \(m=0\).
07-calibration-and-characterization.answer: (a) The slope is \(0.002\) per gate, an accumulating error such as relaxation-induced or coherent leakage into \(\ket1\) per gate; the intercept \(0.10\) is a fixed contribution independent of the number of gates. (b) No: a bad preparation and a detector offset both add a constant at \(m=0\). (c) Measure the readout alone with a heralded or independently verified state, or prepare \(\ket1\) and compare \(p_{\rm report}(1)\) with the expected value; alternatively vary the readout (integration, threshold) while keeping the preparation fixed. Sensitivity to different parameters is what separates causes.

07-calibration-and-characterization.question: Two calibrations are expected to give survival probabilities differing by \(0.005\) near \(p=0.9\). (a) How many shots per calibration are needed for the difference to equal two standard deviations? (b) If the experiment drifts by \(0.01\) per hour and each calibration takes an hour when run sequentially, what bias results? (c) How does interleaving fix it?
hints: The difference of two fractions has variance \(2p(1-p)/N\).
07-calibration-and-characterization.answer: (a) \(2\sqrt{2\times0.09/N}\le0.005\) gives \(N\ge4\times0.18/2.5\times10^{-5}\approx2.9\times10^4\) shots each. (b) Running the second calibration an hour after the first shifts its result by \(0.01\) relative to the first, twice the effect being measured. (c) Alternating short blocks of the two sequences makes both experience the same drift, so the difference is unbiased to first order; comparing blocks over time also measures the drift itself.

07-calibration-and-characterization.question: A student reports: “Process tomography shows my gate has fidelity \(99.9\%\), so its error is \(10^{-3}\).” The tomography assumed perfect preparation and measurement bases, which were calibrated using the same gate. Explain how the result can be misleading, and name a method less sensitive to this problem.
hints: If the reference pulses share the gate’s error, the error appears as part of the reference.
Which method is insensitive to fixed preparation and readout errors?
07-calibration-and-characterization.answer: Tomography reconstructs a process relative to the preparations and measurements used. If those were built with the same miscalibrated pulse, part of the gate error is absorbed into the reference frame and disappears from the reconstruction, while preparation and readout errors can be wrongly attributed to the gate. The reported \(99.9\%\) is then a statement about consistency, not accuracy. Randomized benchmarking estimates average error from how survival decays with sequence length, so fixed preparation and measurement errors enter only the offsets; it still relies on its own assumptions (stationary, gate-independent noise).

07-calibration-and-characterization.question: Resolve the Ramsey sign ambiguity by measuring with two analysis phases, giving \(P_c=\frac12[1+V\cos(\Delta t)]\) and \(P_s=\frac12[1+V\sin(\Delta t)]\) (ignoring decay). (a) At \(t=0.5\) μs, what do the two signals give for \(\Delta/2\pi=+0.5\) MHz and \(-0.5\) MHz? (b) How do the two signals together determine \(\Delta t\) modulo \(2\pi\)? (c) Why is this called quadrature detection?
07-calibration-and-characterization.answer: (a) For \(+0.5\) MHz, \(\Delta t=\pi/2\): \(P_c=\frac12\), \(P_s=\frac12(1+V)\). For \(-0.5\) MHz: \(P_c=\frac12\), \(P_s=\frac12(1-V)\). The cosine signal is identical; the sine signal differs. (b) \((2P_c-1,2P_s-1)=V(\cos\Delta t,\sin\Delta t)\) is a point on a circle of radius \(V\), whose angle is \(\Delta t\) with its sign. (c) The two analysis phases differ by \(\pi/2\) and measure the two quadratures of the precessing phase, just as an I/Q demodulator measures a signal’s in-phase and quadrature components.

07-calibration-and-characterization.question: Show that for the depolarizing channel \(\mathcal D(\rho)=\alpha\rho+(1-\alpha)I/2\), the fidelity with a pure input is \((1+\alpha)/2\) for every input, and that after \(m\) applications the Bloch vector shrinks by \(\alpha^m\). Then explain why randomizing the gates with random Cliffords tends to make an arbitrary error look depolarizing, and name one error type for which this description fails.
hints: Random Cliffords average an error over all directions.
07-calibration-and-characterization.answer: For pure \(\ket\psi\), \(\bra\psi\mathcal D(\ket\psi\bra\psi)\ket\psi=\alpha+(1-\alpha)\frac12=\frac{1+\alpha}{2}\), independent of \(\psi\). Writing \(\rho=\frac12(I+\vec r\cdot\vec\sigma)\), \(\mathcal D\) maps \(\vec r\to\alpha\vec r\), so \(m\) applications give \(\alpha^m\vec r\). Random Cliffords rotate the error into random directions on each step, and averaging over them washes out any preferred axis, leaving an isotropic shrinkage: the depolarizing form. The description fails for leakage, which leaves the qubit space, and for errors that drift during the experiment or depend strongly on which gate is applied.

08-superconducting-circuits.question: An LC resonator has \(L=10\) nH and \(C=100\) fF. Find its frequency \(f=1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC})\). Why can it not serve as a qubit by itself?
hints: Its quantized levels are equally spaced.
08-superconducting-circuits.answer: \(\sqrt{LC}=3.16\times10^{-11}\) s, so \(f\approx5.0\) GHz. Its quantized levels are equally spaced, \(\hbar\omega(n+\frac12)\), so a drive resonant with \(0\to1\) is also resonant with \(1\to2\) and every higher transition. Without nonlinearity no frequency selects a two-level subspace; the Josephson junction supplies that nonlinearity.

08-superconducting-circuits.question: A transmon has \(E_J/h=16\) GHz and \(E_C/h=0.25\) GHz. Estimate \(f_{01}\), \(f_{12}\), and the anharmonicity from \(\hbar\omega_{01}\simeq\sqrt{8E_JE_C}-E_C\). Is \(E_J/E_C\) in the transmon regime?
08-superconducting-circuits.answer: \(\sqrt{8E_JE_C}/h\approx5.66\) GHz, so \(f_{01}\approx5.41\) GHz, \(f_{12}\approx5.16\) GHz, and the anharmonicity is about \(-250\) MHz. \(E_J/E_C=64\), well inside the regime where the quartic expansion is a reasonable approximation and charge sensitivity is strongly suppressed.

08-superconducting-circuits.question: A transmon is coupled to a readout resonator with \(g/2\pi=50\) MHz and detuning \(\Delta/2\pi=1\) GHz. Estimate the dispersive shift scale \(\chi=g^2/\Delta\), and check the condition for the approximation.
08-superconducting-circuits.answer: \(\chi/2\pi=2500/1000=2.5\) MHz. The ratio \(g/\Delta=0.05\) is small, so the two-level dispersive expansion is reasonable here (the transmon’s higher levels modify the exact value). A shift of a few megahertz, compared with a resonator linewidth of similar size, lets a probe tone acquire a clearly different phase for the two qubit states.

08-superconducting-circuits.question: Verify the transmon spectrum from the quartic correction \(-E_C(6n^2+6n+3)/12\). (a) Evaluate it for \(n=0,1,2\). (b) Add the harmonic part \(\sqrt{8E_JE_C}(n+\frac12)\) and compute \(E_1-E_0\) and \(E_2-E_1\). (c) Show that the anharmonicity is \(-E_C\), and evaluate everything for \(E_J/h=20\) GHz, \(E_C/h=0.25\) GHz.
08-superconducting-circuits.answer: (a) \(n=0\): \(-0.25E_C\); \(n=1\): \(-1.25E_C\); \(n=2\): \(-3.25E_C\). (b) \(E_1-E_0=\sqrt{8E_JE_C}-E_C\) and \(E_2-E_1=\sqrt{8E_JE_C}-2E_C\). (c) Their difference is \(-E_C\). With the given values, \(\sqrt{8E_JE_C}/h\approx6.325\) GHz, so \(f_{01}\approx6.075\) GHz, \(f_{12}\approx5.825\) GHz, and the anharmonicity is \(-250\) MHz, as quoted in Section 8.2.1. The level spacing shrinks by \(E_C\) at each step because the cosine potential is softer than a parabola.

08-superconducting-circuits.question: For a qubit-resonator pair with \(g/2\pi=100\) MHz and \(\Delta/2\pi=500\) MHz, (a) compute the exact level shift \(\sqrt{\Delta^2/4+g^2}-\Delta/2\) and compare it with the dispersive estimate \(g^2/\Delta\). (b) Repeat for \(\Delta/2\pi=200\) MHz. (c) What goes wrong as \(g/\Delta\) grows?
08-superconducting-circuits.answer: (a) Exact: \(\sqrt{62500+10000}-250\approx19.3\) MHz; dispersive: \(20\) MHz, about \(4\%\) too large. (b) Exact: \(\sqrt{20000}-100\approx41.4\) MHz; dispersive: \(50\) MHz, \(21\%\) too large. (c) At \(g/\Delta=0.5\) the eigenstates are strongly mixed qubit-resonator states, so “qubit state” and “resonator photon” are no longer separate, the readout photons can drive qubit transitions, and the qubit inherits the resonator’s loss. The dispersive regime trades signal size for clean, nondemolition readout.

08-superconducting-circuits.question: A two-qubit gate gives the state \(\ket{11}\) an extra energy \(\delta E/h=2\) MHz. (a) How long must it act to give a controlled phase \(\pi\)? (b) When the gate is off, a residual \(ZZ\) shift of \(\zeta/2\pi=100\) kHz remains. What conditional phase builds up during \(1\) μs of idling? (c) How does this affect \(\ket{++}\)?
08-superconducting-circuits.answer: (a) \(2\pi\times2\ \text{MHz}\times t=\pi\) gives \(t=250\) ns. (b) \(2\pi\times0.1\ \text{MHz}\times1\ \mu\mathrm s\approx0.63\) rad of unwanted conditional phase, a fifth of a controlled-\(Z\). (c) The idle state \(\ket{++}\) becomes partly entangled, with \(|\alpha_{00}\alpha_{11}-\alpha_{01}\alpha_{10}|=\frac14|e^{-i\phi}-1|\approx0.15\). Residual always-on coupling turns idle time into an error that depends on the neighbors’ states, so it must be suppressed, echoed away, or included in the schedule.

08-superconducting-circuits.question: Estimate cryogenic wiring loads: each control line deposits \(10\) nW at a cold stage. (a) A \(100\)-qubit processor uses \(3\) lines per qubit. What is the load? (b) A \(5000\)-qubit processor with the same wiring? (c) If the stage can absorb \(20\) μW, how many qubits fit, and what design changes would raise the limit?
08-superconducting-circuits.answer: (a) \(300\) lines give \(3\) μW. (b) \(15000\) lines give \(150\) μW. (c) At \(30\) nW per qubit, \(20\) μW supports about \(670\) qubits, before counting active dissipation in amplifiers or the heat conducted by the cables themselves. Raising the limit requires fewer lines per qubit (multiplexed readout, shared control), lower-loss lines, or control electronics placed at warmer stages or made cryogenic. These figures are illustrative, but the scaling is real: wiring grows with qubit count.

08-superconducting-circuits.question: A student argues: “Increasing the qubit-resonator coupling \(g\) always improves readout, because \(\chi=g^2/\Delta\) grows.” Using the exact shifts from the worked problem above, explain why this is not true, and name two costs of large \(g/\Delta\).
hints: At \(g/\Delta=0.5\), the dispersive formula is \(21\%\) off.
The qubit inherits loss from the resonator.
08-superconducting-circuits.answer: At small \(g/\Delta\), \(\chi\) does grow as \(g^2/\Delta\), but by \(g/\Delta=0.5\) the dispersive formula is far off and the qubit and resonator are strongly hybridized. Costs include the qubit decaying through the resonator (Purcell decay), measurement photons inducing qubit transitions, and a stronger dependence of \(\chi\) on probe power. Good readout needs \(\chi\) comparable to the resonator linewidth while staying in the dispersive regime, often with filters to block Purcell decay.

08-superconducting-circuits.question: Two coupled transmons can suffer a frequency collision when an unwanted transition of one is resonant with a transition of the other. Qubit A has \(f_{01}=5.00\) GHz and \(f_{12}=4.70\) GHz; qubit B has \(f_{01}=4.70\) GHz. (a) Which process becomes resonant, and why is it harmful? (b) Propose a frequency for B that avoids collisions with A’s \(f_{01}\) and \(f_{12}\) by at least \(100\) MHz while staying within \(0.5\) GHz of A. (c) Why does this make large arrays hard to lay out?
hints: Exchange can swap an excitation between A’s \(1\to2\) and B’s \(0\to1\).
08-superconducting-circuits.answer: (a) B’s \(0\to1\) is resonant with A’s \(1\to2\). Through exchange, the state \(\ket{1_A1_B}\) can turn into \(\ket{2_A0_B}\), leaking A out of the qubit subspace during any operation that populates \(\ket{11}\). (b) B must avoid \(5.00\pm0.10\) and \(4.70\pm0.10\) GHz; choosing \(f_{01}^B=4.85\) GHz works, \(150\) MHz from both. (c) Each qubit must avoid collisions with every neighbor’s transitions, and fabrication scatter in junction energies shifts frequencies by tens of megahertz, so many fixed-frequency qubits quickly run out of safe frequency space. This motivates tunable couplers, careful frequency allocation, and post-fabrication trimming.

08-superconducting-circuits.question: A qubit coupled to a readout resonator can decay through it at the Purcell rate \(\Gamma_P\approx\kappa(g/\Delta)^2\), where \(\kappa\) is the resonator’s energy decay rate. (a) For \(\kappa/2\pi=5\) MHz and \(g/\Delta=0.05\), find \(\Gamma_P/2\pi\) and the corresponding \(T_1\) limit. (b) How does increasing \(\kappa\) for faster readout affect it? (c) What is the role of a Purcell filter?
08-superconducting-circuits.answer: (a) \(\Gamma_P/2\pi=12.5\) kHz, so \(T_1\le1/(2\pi\times12.5\ \text{kHz})\approx13\) μs, a severe limit for a modern qubit. (b) Readout speed grows with \(\kappa\), but so does Purcell decay, linearly: faster readout costs coherence. (c) A Purcell filter passes signals near the resonator frequency to the amplifier while blocking emission at the qubit frequency, breaking this trade-off so that \(\kappa\) can be large without shortening \(T_1\).

09-trapped-ions.question: Find the zero-point length \(x_0=\sqrt{\hbar/(2m\nu)}\) for an ion of mass \(171\) atomic mass units in a trap with \(\nu/2\pi=2\) MHz. How does it compare with the \(40\)-amu, \(1\) MHz example of the text, and with an optical wavelength?
09-trapped-ions.answer: \(x_0=\sqrt{1.05\times10^{-34}/(2\times2.84\times10^{-25}\times1.26\times10^7)}\approx3.8\) nm. The heavier ion in a stiffer trap is about three times more tightly localized than the \(11\) nm example, since \(x_0\propto(m\nu)^{-1/2}\). Both are far smaller than optical wavelengths of hundreds of nanometres, which is what makes the Lamb–Dicke expansion possible.

09-trapped-ions.question: A thermal motional mode has mean occupation \(\bar n=0.5\). Find \(P_0\), \(P_1\), and the probability of two or more quanta. Is this mode ready for a gate that requires the motional ground state?
09-trapped-ions.answer: \(r=1/3\), so \(P_0=2/3\), \(P_1=2/9\approx0.22\), and \(P_{\ge2}=1-P_0-P_1=1/9\approx0.11\). A third of the time the mode is not in its ground state, so a gate that relies on \(n=0\) would err often; further sideband cooling is needed, unless the gate is designed to tolerate thermal motion.

09-trapped-ions.question: For a \(729\) nm beam along the trap axis and \(x_0=11\) nm, estimate \(\eta=kx_0\) and the Lamb–Dicke parameter \(\eta\sqrt{2n+1}\) for \(n=0\) and \(n=5\). For which occupations is the first-order expansion reliable?
09-trapped-ions.answer: \(\eta\approx8.6\times10^6\times1.1\times10^{-8}\approx0.095\). At \(n=0\), \(\eta\sqrt1\approx0.095\); at \(n=5\), \(\eta\sqrt{11}\approx0.31\). The expansion \(e^{i\eta(a+a^\dagger)}\approx1+i\eta(a+a^\dagger)\) is reliable when this is well below \(1\): good for the ground state and the lowest few levels, increasingly poor for warmer motion, where higher-order sidebands appear.

09-trapped-ions.question: Red-sideband Rabi frequencies scale as \(\eta\Omega\sqrt n\). Take \(\eta\Omega/2\pi=10\) kHz. (a) Find the red-sideband \(\pi\)-pulse times for \(n=1\) and \(n=4\). (b) A pulse tuned to be a \(\pi\) pulse for \(n=1\) is applied to \(\ket{0,4}\). What rotation angle results, and how much population is transferred? (c) Why does this complicate cooling a thermal state with fixed pulses?
hints: For \(n=4\) the rotation angle is \(\sqrt4\) times larger.
09-trapped-ions.answer: (a) \(n=1\): \(t_\pi=1/(2\times10\ \text{kHz})=50\) μs. \(n=4\): \(25\) μs. (b) The \(50\) μs pulse rotates \(\ket{0,4}\) by \(2\pi\), returning it to where it started: no transfer. (c) Each occupation number has its own Rabi frequency, so no single pulse removes a quantum from every \(n\). Cooling protocols use sequences of pulses with different durations, or continuous cooling with dissipation, to work across the thermal distribution.

09-trapped-ions.question: In the motion-mediated gate, the closed-trajectory operation is \(e^{i\Phi S^2}\) with \(S=X_1+X_2\) and \(\Phi(T)=2\pi g^2/\delta^2\). (a) Using \(S^2=2I+2X_1X_2\), write the operation as a global phase times \(e^{2i\Phi X_1X_2}\). (b) Find \(g/\delta\) that makes it maximally entangling, \(e^{i\frac\pi4X_1X_2}\). (c) Apply it to \(\ket{00}\), and give the gate time in terms of \(g\).
09-trapped-ions.answer: (a) \(e^{i\Phi S^2}=e^{2i\Phi}\,e^{2i\Phi X_1X_2}\). (b) Setting \(2\Phi=\pi/4\) gives \(\Phi=\pi/8\), so \(2\pi g^2/\delta^2=\pi/8\) and \(g/\delta=1/4\), the value used in the figure. (c) \(e^{i\frac\pi4X_1X_2}\ket{00}=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket{00}+i\ket{11})\), a maximally entangled state. The gate time is \(T=2\pi/\delta=2\pi/(4g)=\pi/(2g)\): a stronger force gives a faster gate, with the detuning scaled to keep \(g/\delta=1/4\).

09-trapped-ions.question: Fluorescence counts are Poisson. A bright ion gives mean \(\mu_b=10\) counts and a dark ion a background mean \(\mu_d=0.05\). (a) With threshold “at least one count means bright,” find the probabilities of missing a bright ion and of a false bright. (b) Repeat for threshold “at least two counts.” (c) Which threshold is better here?
09-trapped-ions.answer: (a) Missed bright: \(e^{-10}\approx4.5\times10^{-5}\). False bright: \(1-e^{-0.05}\approx0.049\). (b) Missed bright: \(e^{-10}(1+10)\approx5.0\times10^{-4}\). False bright: \(1-e^{-0.05}(1.05)\approx1.2\times10^{-3}\). (c) The two-count threshold gives a total error near \(1.7\times10^{-3}\), against about \(0.049\) for the one-count threshold. Background counts, not missed photons, dominate at the low threshold. The best threshold balances both error types for the actual count distributions.

09-trapped-ions.question: Two ion registers are linked by heralded photonic entanglement with success probability \(s=10^{-4}\) per attempt and attempt duration \(\tau=1\) μs. (a) Find the mean waiting time. (b) What is the probability that the wait exceeds three times the mean? (c) What memory coherence time is needed for the stored qubits to keep fidelity above \(0.99\) during a typical wait, assuming exponential decay of coherence?
09-trapped-ions.answer: (a) \(\tau/s=10\) ms. (b) \(P(\text{wait}>30\ \text{ms})\approx e^{-3}\approx0.05\). (c) Requiring \(e^{-t/T_2}\ge0.99\) at \(t=10\) ms gives \(T_2\ge-10\ \text{ms}/\ln0.99\approx1\) s, and a longer one to cover the slow tail. Local gates take microseconds, but a remote link adds milliseconds of waiting, so memory coherence, not gate speed, can set the performance of a networked architecture.

09-trapped-ions.question: A student says: “The Lamb–Dicke approximation holds because \(\eta=0.1\ll1\).” Check \(\eta\sqrt{2n+1}\) for an ion with \(\bar n=50\) (Doppler-cooled, not ground-state cooled). What happens to carrier and sideband transitions, and what condition really matters?
hints: The expansion is in powers of \(\eta(a+a^\dagger)\), whose size grows with \(n\).
09-trapped-ions.answer: \(\eta\sqrt{2n+1}\approx0.1\times10=1.0\): not small. The first-order expansion fails, higher-order sidebands become significant, and the carrier Rabi frequency itself depends on \(n\) through factors like \(1-\eta^2n\). A thermal distribution then spreads the Rabi frequencies, blurring oscillations and degrading gates. The relevant condition is \(\eta^2(2n+1)\ll1\) for the occupations actually present, which is why ground-state cooling matters even when \(\eta\) is small.

09-trapped-ions.question:
Two ions in a linear trap have two axial modes: the centre-of-mass mode at \(
u\) and the stretch mode at \(\sqrt3
u\). (a) For \(
u/2\pi=1\) MHz, how far apart in frequency are their red sidebands? (b) If the sideband Rabi frequency is \(\eta\Omega/2\pi=20\) kHz, estimate how strongly a pulse resonant with the centre-of-mass sideband drives the stretch sideband, using \(\Omega^2/(\Omega^2+\Delta^2)\). (c) What happens to this separation as more ions are added?
09-trapped-ions.answer: (a) The sidebands are separated by \((\sqrt3-1)\times1\ \text{MHz}\approx0.73\) MHz. (b) \(\Delta/(\eta\Omega)\approx730/20\approx37\), so the off-resonant excitation is bounded by about \(1/(1+37^2)\approx7\times10^{-4}\). (c) With \(N\) ions there are \(N\) axial modes packed into a frequency range that does not grow proportionally, so the spacing between neighbouring modes shrinks. Resolving a single mode then needs weaker, slower drives, or pulse shaping that closes the trajectory of every mode, which is one reason long single chains are hard to scale.

09-trapped-ions.question: Explain why the ideal motion-mediated gate works for any initial motional state, not only the ground state. The propagator in the ideal model is a spin-dependent displacement \(D(\alpha(t)S)\) times \(e^{i\Phi(t)S^2}\). (a) What is \(D(\alpha S)\) at the closure time \(T\)? (b) Why does the result not depend on the initial motional state? (c) What effects break this insensitivity in practice?
hints: \(D(0)\) is the identity on the motion.
09-trapped-ions.answer: (a) At \(T=2\pi/\delta\), \(\alpha(T)=0\), so the displacement is the identity for every eigenvalue of \(S\). (b) The remaining operator \(e^{i\Phi S^2}\) acts only on the spins, and \(\Phi\) does not involve the motional state, so every initial motional state, thermal or not, ends unchanged and disentangled from the spins.
